# Decision history — templartorrent

Every revision of every decision, plus the terminal revisions of other normative records. Includes archived records: this is the project's memory of what it used to think.

## templartorrent.decision.fork-rbit-for-native-gate

### Revision 1 — Fork rbit 0.2.2 in-tree to drop reqwest/rustls/ring; announce over an application-owned HTTP transport

`proposed` · `@templartorrent.decision.fork-rbit-for-native-gate/1` · scope `path "Cargo.toml"`, `path "integration/rbit-adapter/**"`, `path "vendor/rbit/**"` · topic `rbit-fork`

Vendor rbit 0.2.2 into the repository as a path dependency applied through [patch.crates-io], make its reqwest dependency optional behind a Cargo feature that TemplarTorrent does not enable, and replace rbit::HttpTracker in the adapter with an application-owned bounded plain-HTTP announce client that connects to the already-admitted tracker address. HTTPS trackers are refused with a visible reason until a pure-Rust TLS stack is chosen.

**Context.** The strict native-source audit reported ring 0.17.14 through rbit -> reqwest (rustls-tls) -> rustls -> ring. rbit 0.2.2 as published offers no feature to disable reqwest, which it uses in tracker/http.rs, webseed.rs and upnp.rs. The owner chose the fork option on 2026-10-22 over keeping the gate open or accepting ring as an exception.

**Consequences.** The adapter still depends on the rbit API surface (peer connection, framing, metainfo, bencode, piece hashes) but the version pin becomes a pinned in-tree fork rather than the crates.io artifact, and rbit upgrades require re-applying the feature gate. HTTP tracker announces are now the application's responsibility, including bounded response reading and redirect refusal; webseed and UPnP from rbit are unavailable and were never used.
